extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate students and researchers in combinatorics and graph theory; readers interested in proofs of classical theorems (art gallery theorem, Turán's theorem, Shannon capacity / Lovász bound)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook proofs and constructions in combinatorics/graph theory: the art-gallery theorem (triangulation + 3-coloring), Turán's extremal graph theorem (several proofs), and Shannon capacity / Lovász bound (orthonormal representations and eigenvalue constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art Gallery Theorem (guard-number bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any museum modelled as an n-sided polygon, floor(n/3) guards suffice to see every point (i.e., every point is visible from some guard stationed at a vertex).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof (Fisk): triangulate the polygon (n−3 noncrossing diagonals), regard triangulation as a plane graph, 3-color the vertices of the triangulated graph; one color class has at most floor(n/3) vertices, place guards at those vertices. Every triangle contains a vertex of that color so the entire polygon is guarded. Example / tightness: a comb-shaped museum with n = 3m walls requires m = n/3 guards (lower bound). Notes: triangulation existence is proved by induction via finding a convex vertex and producing a diagonal. Variants: guarding only walls or allowing guards to patrol walls changes bounds (see wall-guard variant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of triangulation for a simple polygon (construction requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any planar (simple) polygon can be triangulated by drawing noncrossing diagonals between vertices until the interior is partitioned into triangles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inductive construction: find a convex vertex A (there are at least three), consider its neighbors B and C; if BC lies inside polygon it's a diagonal; otherwise slide BC toward A until it hits a last vertex Z inside triangle ABC, then AZ is a diagonal. Note: this argument is specific to 2D polygons — triangulation without adding vertices fails in 3D (Schönhardt's polyhedron is a counterexample).

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-colorability of triangulated planar polygon graphs (key lemma for guard placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The planar graph formed by the vertices and edges (walls + triangulation diagonals) of a triangulated polygon is 3-colorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction: for n>3 pick a diagonal uv that splits polygon into two smaller triangulated graphs both containing uv; color each part with 3 colors choosing consistent colors for u and v (e.g., color u as 1 and v as 2) and paste the colorings together. This 3-colorability is the combinatorial fact used to bound number of guards (pick smallest color class).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wall-guard variant (patrolling along walls)
rubrics_metrics.description: If each guard may patrol one wall (walk along that wall and sees anything visible from any point on it), certain polygons require floor(n/4) wall-guards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Toussaint constructed polygons (e.g., with 4m sides) where m wall-guards are necessary; conjectured (but unproven) that except for small n this number is also sufficient. Guidance: design examples to show lower bounds; proof of sufficiency remains open in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turán's theorem (extremal edge bound for Kp-free graphs)
rubrics_metrics.description: If G is a simple graph on n vertices that contains no p-clique (p≥2), then |E| ≤ (1 - 1/(p−1)) * n^2 / 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equality is attained by the Turán graphs Kn1,...,n_{p−1} formed by partitioning V into p−1 parts (as equal as possible, |ni − nj| ≤ 1) and joining all pairs of vertices from distinct parts. Construction guidance: to maximize number of edges under the p-clique-free constraint, distribute vertex counts as evenly as possible among the p−1 parts (shifting a vertex from a larger to a smaller part strictly increases edges when imbalance ≥2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of extremal graphs (Turán graphs and balanced partition condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among Kp-free graphs on n vertices, graphs maximizing edge count are complete (p−1)-partite graphs with part sizes differing by at most 1 (the Turán graphs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument sketches: multiple proofs (see below) show uniqueness of extremal structure. Practical construction: partition n into p−1 parts as evenly as possible and connect all inter-part pairs to obtain maximal edges. Anti-pattern: leaving large imbalance among parts can be improved by moving vertices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turán — proof by induction using a (p−1)-clique (first proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive proof of Turán's inequality: pick a (p−1)-clique A in a maximal-edge Kp-free graph G; let B = V ar{A}; bound edges inside B by induction and edges between A and B by (p−2)|B| to obtain the desired global bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use eB ≤ (1 − 1/(p−1))(n − p + 1)^2/2 (induction) and e_{A,B} ≤ (p−2)(n − p + 1) because vertices in B can be adjacent to at most p−2 vertices of A (no p-clique). Sum bounds to derive Turán inequality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turán — structural reduction to complete multipartite form (second proof)
rubrics_metrics.description:
Transform G to a graph H with the same vertex set where T = V 
eighbors(v_m) is made independent and all edges between S and T are present; show |E(H)| ≥ |E(G)| and use induction on |S| to compare with suitable Turán graph to conclude the bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose vertex v_m of maximal degree d_m, set S = N(v_m) and T = V  ackslash S. Construct H that keeps edges in S but makes T independent and adds all S−T edges; H has no p-cliques and |E(H)| ≥ |E(G)|. Then compare with Kn1,...,n_{p−1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motzkin–Straus analytic proof (third proof via maximizing quadratic form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider probability distributions w on vertices and maximize f(w) = sum_{vivj∈E} w_i w_j; show an optimal distribution concentrates weights on a clique and attains value (1/2)(1 − 1/k) on a k-clique; taking k = p−1 yields the Turán bound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight-moving argument: if two nonadjacent vertices have positive weights move weight from one to the other to increase f. Local perturbation shows optimum on equal weights on a clique. Use the uniform distribution to relate f(w) to |E| and deduce upper bound on |E|.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probabilistic/Cauchy–Schwarz proof (fourth proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a random permutation of vertices and consider set C_π of vertices that are adjacent to all earlier vertices; expectation EX = sum_i 1/(n − d_i) gives lower bound on clique size ω(G) ≥ sum 1/(n − d_i). Combine with Cauchy–Schwarz and double-counting sum d_i = 2|E| to get Turán inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use linearity of expectation and the fact that the expected size of the constructed clique equals sum 1/(n − d_i). Apply Cauchy–Schwarz with appropriate ai,bi to connect to n^2 and ω(G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication/forbidden configuration argument (fifth proof and uniqueness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that in an extremal Kp-free graph no configuration of three vertices u,v,w can exist with vw an edge but u nonadjacent to v and w; duplication/deletion operations then imply the adjacency relation is an equivalence relation, so the graph is complete multipartite and hence a Turán graph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two cases: duplicate the higher-degree vertex and delete the lower-degree one to increase edges (contradiction), or duplicate the low-degree vertex twice and delete the other two; both contradictions force the equivalence relation. This gives uniqueness of extremal graphs (Turán graphs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusion graph model for zero-error communication (Shannon model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model a communication channel by a confusion graph G=(V,E): vertices are symbols, edges connect pairs of symbols that may be confused. Error-free single-symbol transmission uses an independent set U ⊆ V; achievable single-symbol rate is log2 α(G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To improve rate, use strings (codewords) of length n; confusion graph for length-n strings is the strong/product graph G^n = G × ... × G where two n-tuples are adjacent if for every coordinate either entries equal or adjacent in original graph. Independent sets in G^n correspond to error-free codebooks for length-n strings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Shannon (zero-error) capacity Θ(G)
rubrics_metrics.description: Θ(G) := sup_{n≥1} α(G^n)^{1/n} (equivalently, sup_n (α(G^n))^{1/n}), and information rate per symbol for length-n strings is log2 (α(G^n))/n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic inequality: α(G^n) ≥ α(G)^n, so Θ(G) ≥ α(G). For specific graphs (e.g., C5) using length-2 strings can increase capacity: α(C5)=2 but α(C5^2)=5 giving Θ(C5) ≥ sqrt(5).

rubrics_metrics.name: LP dual bound λ(G) and multiplicativity
rubrics_metrics.description: Define λ(G) = min_x max_{C clique} sum_{v∈C} x_v where x ranges over probability distributions on vertices. Linear programming duality yields an equivalent max_y min_v sum_{C∋v} y_C representation. λ(G^n) = λ(G)^n and hence α(G^n) ≤ λ(G^n)^{-1} = λ(G)^{-n}, so Θ(G) ≤ λ(G)^{-1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove multiplicativity λ(G×H)=λ(G)λ(H) use product distributions and note maximal cliques in product are products of cliques. This gives a general explicit upper bound for Θ(G) via an LP quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lovász orthonormal-representation bound (Θ(G) ≤ 1/σ_T)
rubrics_metrics.description: If G has an orthonormal representation T = {v(1),...,v(m)} in R^s where nonadjacent vertices correspond to orthogonal unit vectors, and all v(i) have the same inner product σ_T with u := (1/m) sum_i v(i), then Θ(G) ≤ 1/σ_T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch: define μ(x) = |sum_i x_i v(i)|^2 and μ_T(G)=inf_x μ(x). For an independent set U of size α, μ_T(G) ≤ 1/α, so α ≤ 1/μ_T(G). Show μ_T(G)=σ_T by Cauchy–Schwarz and evaluating the uniform distribution, hence α ≤ 1/σ_T. Multiplicativity of the construction over graph products yields Θ(G) ≤ 1/σ_T. Example: Lovász 'umbrella' for C5 gives σ_T = 1/√5 and hence Θ(C5) ≤ √5; combined with lower bound yields Θ(C5)=√5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of orthonormal representation from adjacency matrix (spectral method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given adjacency matrix A of G with smallest eigenvalue −p (p>0), form M = I + (1/p)A which is positive semidefinite; principal axis theorem yields vectors v(i) with (v(i),v(i))=1 and (v(i),v(j)) = a_{ij}/p for i≠j, providing an orthonormal representation with computable constant σ_T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute p = |λ_min| (e.g., for odd cycle Cm, p = 2 cos(π/m)). Row-sums of M and inner products with u give the constant σ_T = (1 + (2/p))/m for cycles, leading to explicit Lovász-type upper bounds (for odd m≥5: Θ(Cm) ≤ (1 + cos(π/m))^{-1}). This spectral construction is the standard method to produce the Lovász umbrella.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eigenvalues of cycle Cm (used in spectral constructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjacency matrix eigenvalues of Cm are 2 cos(2kπ/m) (0 ≤ k ≤ m−1); for odd m the smallest eigenvalue is −2 cos(π/m), so p = 2 cos(π/m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use m-th roots of unity and corresponding eigenvectors (1,λ,λ^2,...). This eigenvalue information feeds into the computation of M = I + (1/p)A and the constant σ_T in the orthonormal representation, thereby yielding explicit bounds for Θ(Cm).
